hints: Look at carbon 2 in $\text{CH}_3(\text{CH}_2)_5\text{CHBrCH}_3$ and count how many different groups are attached to it to decide what type of stereoisomerism is possible.
Recall how to show a tetrahedral carbon in 3D using solid wedge, hashed wedge and straight lines, and think about what must be swapped to make the non-superimposable mirror image.
walkthrough:
Spot the chiral centre**
Look closely at $\text{CH}_3(\text{CH}_2)_5\text{CHBrCH}_3$. Focus on the $\text{CH}$ carbon, that is carbon 2. It is joined to four different things: $\text{H}$, $\text{Br}$, $\text{CH}_3$ and $\text{R}$ where $\text{R} = \text{CH}_3(\text{CH}_2)_5$. Four different groups on one tetrahedral carbon means a chiral centre, so the molecule exists as a pair of enantiomers.

Draw the first enantiomer in 3D**
Put the chiral $\text{C}$ in the centre. Draw two bonds in the plane, for example to $\text{R}$ and to $\text{CH}_3$. Then draw one bond coming out toward you with a solid wedge, for example $\text{Br}$, and one bond going away with a hashed wedge, for example $\text{H}$. That wedge-dash pair is what makes it 3D.

Draw the mirror image**
For the second stereoisomer, keep $\text{R}$ and $\text{CH}_3$ in the same in-plane positions but swap wedge and dash: put $\text{H}$ on the solid wedge and $\text{Br}$ on the hashed wedge. The two structures are mirror images and cannot be superimposed, so they are the pair of enantiomers.

Final answer: Two 3D structures of $\text{RCHBrCH}_3$ where $\text{R} = \text{CH}_3(\text{CH}_2)_5$, each with chiral C bonded to $\text{H}$, $\text{Br}$, $\text{CH}_3$ and $\text{R}$ in tetrahedral arrangement.
One enantiomer has $\text{Br}$ on wedge and $\text{H}$ on dash (or vice versa), the second enantiomer has the positions reversed, giving non-superimposable mirror images.

hints: Remember that $\text{S}_{\text{N}}1$ means substitution in two steps with a carbocation in the middle, so think about which bond breaks first without the $\text{OH}^-$ involved.
Consider why the $\text{C}-\text{Br}$ bond is polar and where the pair of electrons goes when $\text{Br}^-$ leaves.
Think about what the positively charged carbon intermediate looks like and how a lone pair on $\text{OH}^-$ can form the new $\text{C}-\text{OH}$ bond.
walkthrough:
Polarise the leaving group bond**
Bromine is more electronegative than carbon, so the $\text{C}-\text{Br}$ bond is polar: $\text{C}^{\delta+}-\text{Br}^{\delta-}$. In $\text{S}_{\text{N}}1$ the bond breaks by itself first. Draw a curly arrow starting on the $\text{C}-\text{Br}$ bond and pointing onto $\text{Br}$, showing $\text{Br}^-$ leaving.

Form the flat carbocation**
When $\text{Br}^-$ leaves, carbon 2 is left with only three bonds and a positive charge: $\text{CH}_3(\text{CH}_2)_5\text{C}^+\text{(H)CH}_3$. This secondary carbocation is planar and is the key $\text{S}_{\text{N}}1$ intermediate. No $\text{OH}^-$ is involved yet, that is why it is unimolecular.

Attack by hydroxide**
Now the nucleophile acts. The $\text{OH}^-$ ion has lone pairs. Draw a curly arrow from a lone pair on $\text{:OH}^-$ to the positively charged $\text{C}^+$. This makes the new $\text{C}-\text{OH}$ bond and gives the product $\text{CH}_3(\text{CH}_2)_5\text{CH(OH)CH}_3$.

Final answer: Step 1: $\text{C}^{\delta+}-\text{Br}^{\delta-}$ with curly arrow from $\text{C}-\text{Br}$ bond to $\text{Br}$ to give $\text{CH}_3(\text{CH}_2)_5\text{C}^+\text{(H)CH}_3 + \text{Br}^-$.
Step 2: curly arrow from lone pair on $\text{OH}^-$ to $\text{C}^+$ to give $\text{CH}_3(\text{CH}_2)_5\text{CH(OH)CH}_3$.

hints: Match each reagent to the functional group it tests for: $\text{Br}_2$ for $\text{C}=\text{C}$, $\text{PCl}_5$ for $\text{-OH}$, $\text{AgNO}_3\text{(aq)}$ for hydrolysable halide.
Recall the classic positive observations: decolourisation of bromine, steamy fumes of $\text{HCl}$, and cream precipitate of $\text{AgBr}$.
If the functional group is absent, no visible change occurs, so use x for those boxes.
walkthrough:
Use bromine for the alkene**
$\text{Br}_2$ in the dark adds across $\text{C}=\text{C}$ by electrophilic addition. The alkene $\text{CH}_3(\text{CH}_2)_5\text{CHCH}_2$ therefore decolourises orange or brown bromine to colourless. The saturated bromoalkane has no $\text{C}=\text{C}$, so no reaction, write x.

Use PCl5 for the alcohol**
$\text{PCl}_5$ reacts with the $\text{-OH}$ group of octan-2-ol, $\text{CH}_3(\text{CH}_2)_5\text{CH(OH)CH}_3$, to give steamy white fumes of $\text{HCl}$. The alkene has no $\text{-OH}$ group, so no reaction, write x.

Use silver nitrate for the bromoalkane**
On warming with water, 2-bromooctane hydrolyses to release $\text{Br}^-$, which gives a cream or off-white precipitate of $\text{AgBr}$ with $\text{AgNO}_3\text{(aq)}$. The alcohol cannot supply halide ions, so no precipitate, write x.

Final answer: $\text{Br}_2\text{(l)}$ in the dark: with $\text{CH}_3(\text{CH}_2)_5\text{CHBrCH}_3$ x, with $\text{CH}_3(\text{CH}_2)_5\text{CHCH}_2$ orange to colourless.
$\text{PCl}_5\text{(s)}$: with $\text{CH}_3(\text{CH}_2)_5\text{CH(OH)CH}_3$ steamy fumes, with $\text{CH}_3(\text{CH}_2)_5\text{CHCH}_2$ x.
$\text{AgNO}_3\text{(aq)}$: with $\text{CH}_3(\text{CH}_2)_5\text{CHBrCH}_3$ cream precipitate, with $\text{CH}_3(\text{CH}_2)_5\text{CH(OH)CH}_3$ x.

hints: Look at Fig. 4.2: the starting bromoalkane loses $\text{HBr}$ and gains a $\text{C}=\text{C}$ bond to give three octenes.
walkthrough:
Recognise loss of HBr to form C=C**
Start with $\text{CH}_3(\text{CH}_2)_5\text{CHBrCH}_3$ and end with alkenes E, F and G. You have removed $\text{H}$ and $\text{Br}$ from adjacent carbons and formed a double bond. That is the definition of an elimination reaction.
Final answer: elimination (dehydrohalogenation)

hints: Recall the choice between aqueous $\text{NaOH}$ for substitution to an alcohol and alcoholic $\text{NaOH}$ for elimination to an alkene.
walkthrough:
Pick conditions that favour elimination**
Aqueous $\text{NaOH}$ would give substitution to the alcohol. To force elimination of $\text{HBr}$ to an alkene you use $\text{NaOH}$ dissolved in ethanol, with heating. The ethanol solvent and heat favour removal of $\text{H}^+$ rather than attack by $\text{OH}^-$.
Final answer: $\text{NaOH}$ in ethanol, heated

hints: Count the total carbons in E (oct-2-ene) and identify which carbons are part of the $\text{C}=\text{C}$ double bond.
Link double bonded carbons to $sp^2$ and singly bonded tetrahedral carbons to $sp^3$, remembering there is no triple bond for $sp$.
walkthrough:
Sort the carbons in E**
E is $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}=\text{CHCH}_3$, an 8-carbon alkene. The two carbons in the $\text{C}=\text{C}$ bond each have three sigma regions and one pi bond, so they are $sp^2$ hybridised. That gives 2.

Count the rest**
The other six carbons are all bonded by four single sigma bonds in tetrahedral geometry, so they are $sp^3$ hybridised. There is no $\text{C}\equiv\text{C}$ triple bond, so $sp = 0$. Hence 0, 2 and 6.
Final answer: sp hybridised: 0; $sp^2$ hybridised: 2; $sp^3$ hybridised: 6

hints: Think about which bond type in an alkene is different from an alkane and what it stops the molecule doing.
Consider why rotation about $\text{C}-\text{C}$ is easy but rotation about $\text{C}=\text{C}$ would require breaking a bond.
Ask what must be attached to each $\text{C}=\text{C}$ carbon for the two spatial arrangements to be genuinely different.
walkthrough:
Need a pi bond**
The essential feature is a $\text{C}=\text{C}$ double bond. It contains a $\sigma$ bond plus a $\pi$ bond formed by sideways overlap of p orbitals above and below the bond axis.

Lock the rotation**
In an alkane you can freely rotate about a $\text{C}-\text{C}$ $\sigma$ bond. In an alkene, twisting about $\text{C}=\text{C}$ would break the $\pi$ overlap, which needs a lot of energy. So rotation is restricted or prevented, locking substituents in fixed positions.

Need two different groups on each carbon**
Locking alone is not enough. Each doubly bonded carbon must carry two different atoms or groups, for example $\text{H}$ and an alkyl chain in oct-2-ene. Then swapping their spatial positions gives distinct cis/trans or E/Z stereoisomers that cannot interconvert.

Final answer: Presence of a $\text{C}=\text{C}$ double bond containing a $\pi$ bond.
Restricted rotation about the $\text{C}=\text{C}$ bond.
Each $\text{C}=\text{C}$ carbon bonded to two different groups (e.g. $\text{H}$ and alkyl), giving E/Z or cis/trans isomers.
